caption:
A false positive is not free. Every alert dispatches a patrol, a duty officer, an hour of attention that could have gone to a real signature. Run the threshold too loose and the queue fills with noise until operators start ignoring it — the same failure mode as no coverage at all.

Run it too tight and the system misses the slow, low-signature change that matters: a pipeline tap that bleeds for weeks, a reservoir creeping past its rule curve. Tuning that line is not a technical afterthought. It is the difference between a system commanders trust and one they route around.

The honest measure of a monitoring system is not how many alerts it generates. It is how many of those alerts were worth the trip.
thread: A false positive is not free. It costs a patrol, a duty officer's hour, attention pulled from a real signature.
Set the alert threshold too loose and the queue fills with noise. Operators learn to ignore it. That is the same failure as no coverage — just slower to notice.
Set it too tight and you miss the slow bleed: a tap that drains for weeks, a reservoir edging past its rule curve, never enough change in one pass to trip the alarm.
The real measure of a monitoring system isn't alert volume. It's the fraction of alerts worth the trip out.

card.headline: An alert that isn't worth the trip is a cost
card.sub: Loose thresholds drown operators in noise. Tight ones miss the slow bleed. Tuning that line is the job.

rationale: Fills the one untouched EXPLAINER angle in the brief — false-positive cost — without repeating prior cadence/radar/cause posts, and stays instructive rather than promotional.
